content:
Local weather is one of the most underrated variables in Apple Home smart home automation setups. Over the past few years, I have used various sensors, from dripping faucets on freezing days to using Eve Aqua to adjust sprinkler schedules on hot days, and have applied them all. Eve Weather has been part of my setup for a while, and since it upgraded to support Matter a few years ago, it has been really useful at home.

HomeKit Weekly is a专题 series that focuses on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything related to the Apple smart home framework.

If you have been following HomeKit Weekly, you know I like automation designs that run on their own. Smart home accessories are only truly useful when they can execute tasks automatically. That is why I always recommend building your smart home around a single ecosystem rather than mixing and matching. Even though we are in the Matter era, I still don't want to use a bunch of different platforms. For me, the answer is Apple Home. I prefer Eve devices because they have always placed a strong emphasis on privacy, and as long as you stick with local control combined with Matter, you don't need to sign up for any extra cloud accounts. Eve has also been very active in supporting Matter and Thread in recent years. These are exactly the kind of developments you want to see.

Eve Weather is a compact device that gives you three data points: temperature, humidity, and barometric pressure. It has an IPX4 waterproof rating, and its aluminum casing design fits in perfectly when placed outdoors. My unit is installed right outside. What it provides are readings that are very close to the actual conditions on the ground, and they often differ from Apple Weather data by several degrees. Honestly, that few degrees difference can be critical in extreme heat or severe cold. When your home's water pipes freeze at 31 degrees Fahrenheit, but your app shows it is still 34 degrees, you will be glad you installed this local sensor.

One of the underrated features of Eve Weather is its built-in 12-hour weather trend display. It uses barometric pressure changes to forecast weather trends, showing icons for expected sunny, cloudy, rainy, or stormy conditions. This small detail is very practical, letting you see at a glance without having to open a phone app.

Here are a few examples of automations you can set up using Eve Weather:

  • When the temperature drops below freezing, turn on a colored light to remind people at home to let the faucets drip.
  • When outdoor humidity is particularly high, turn on the dehumidifier.
  • If it has already rained and the forecast shows more rain, delay activating the sprinkler system.
  • Without leaving the house, ask Siri how many degrees it is in the front yard right now.

Matter and Thread support in 2026

A few years ago, Eve released a free firmware update that added Matter support to Eve Weather. If you already own this device, you can upgrade through the Eve app. The Matter version supports Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and SmartThings in addition to Apple Home. The sensor itself is exactly the same; it just becomes cross-platform compatible, so you won't have to worry about switching your main smart home ecosystem in the future.

Eve Weather is a so-called 'Minimal Thread Device'. This means it can communicate via Thread, but it does not relay data. That task is left to always-on 'Full Thread Devices' such as Eve Energy or Eve Water Guard. The more Full Thread Devices you have in your home, the more stable the Thread network will be, and battery-powered devices like Eve Weather will directly benefit from this stability.

You still don't need an Eve account. Unless you actively choose to, all data stays local. The Eve iPhone app is a great tool for visualizing historical trends in temperature, barometric pressure, and humidity. Using it to analyze patterns and make smarter decisions about when to water the lawn or manage electricity usage is quite interesting.

I have several HomePod minis placed throughout my home, and I rely on my home's Eero 6E network to support Thread. Eero has built-in Thread support, providing a stable connection foundation for accessories like Eve Weather and ensuring smooth operation.

Summary after using Eve Weather

The only thing I still hope to see improved is switching to a rechargeable battery. Although the current battery life can last several months, I would prefer it to come with a USB-C port like the Eve Room. Apart from that, Eve Weather is definitely one of my favorite Apple Home accessories. The design is simple and looks great, and thanks to Matter, it works well across all major platforms. If you want to add local weather information to your smart home and pair it with practical automations, Eve Weather is, for me, an unequivocal recommendation.

You can buy it directly from Amazon or the Eve official online store.
